title: How to Grow Basil and Other Kitchen Herbs in Pots
topic: làm vườn: trồng húng quế và rau thơm trong chậu
summary: Why supermarket basil dies, how to pinch a plant so it grows bushy, and how to keep mint, coriander, rosemary and Vietnamese herbs like rau răm and ngò gai thriving on a windowsill or balcony.
body:
There is a particular pleasure in reaching out of a kitchen window, pinching off a few leaves of basil, and dropping them into a pan a minute later. The smell is sharper than anything in a supermarket packet, the leaves have not had time to wilt, and the plant that gave them will grow more. A small pot of herbs is also one of the most forgiving ways to start gardening. You do not need a garden, a lot of money or special skills. A sunny windowsill, a balcony railing or a strip of concrete by the door will do.

That said, many first attempts end badly. The basil bought in a pot from the supermarket collapses within two weeks. The mint takes over everything. The coriander shoots up into flower almost as soon as it has leaves. These failures are not bad luck. They come from a handful of predictable mistakes, and once you understand what each herb wants, they become easy to avoid.

This guide focuses on basil, the classic kitchen herb, and then widens out to other herbs worth growing in containers, including several that are central to Vietnamese and wider Southeast Asian cooking. It covers choosing pots and soil, sowing and buying plants, light and water, how to harvest so the plant keeps producing, and how to deal with the common problems. Growing conditions vary hugely between climates, so treat the numbers here as starting points and watch your own plants.

## Why herbs suit containers

Most culinary herbs are small, fast-growing plants that you harvest a little at a time. That makes them ideal for pots. A container lets you put the plant exactly where the light is best, move it out of harsh weather, control the soil, and keep aggressive spreaders like mint from escaping. It also puts the herbs within arm's reach of the kitchen, which matters more than people think: herbs that are close by get used, and herbs that get used are harvested regularly, which, as we will see, is exactly what keeps many of them healthy.

There are a few trade-offs. Soil in a pot dries out much faster than soil in the ground, it heats up more in summer sun, and nutrients wash out with every watering. A potted plant depends on you entirely. But those are manageable problems, and the rest of this guide is mostly about managing them.

## Getting to know basil

Sweet basil, *Ocimum basilicum*, belongs to the mint family, Lamiaceae, along with many other aromatic herbs such as mint, rosemary, thyme, oregano, sage and perilla. You can often recognise members of this family by their square stems and leaves arranged in opposite pairs. Basil is native to tropical regions of Asia and Africa, and that origin explains almost everything about how it behaves.

Basil loves **heat and sun**. It grows slowly and sulks in cool weather, and it is very sensitive to cold. Temperatures near freezing will blacken and kill it, and even a spell of cool nights in the range of about 10°C can damage leaves and stop growth. In temperate climates it is grown as a summer annual and should not go outside until nights are reliably warm. In tropical and subtropical places, including much of Vietnam, basil grows readily for much of the year, though intense midday heat and heavy monsoon rain bring their own challenges.

Basil is also an **annual** in practice. Its natural goal is to grow, flower, set seed and die within a season. A lot of good basil care is really about persuading the plant to delay that final stage so that it keeps making leaves.

There are many varieties. The large-leaved Genovese type is the classic for Italian cooking and pesto. Thai basil, known in Vietnamese as *húng quế*, has smaller leaves, purple stems and flowers, and a distinct anise or liquorice note; it is the basil served with phở in southern Vietnam. Holy basil, *Ocimum tenuiflorum*, called *tulsi* in India, has a peppery, clove-like taste and is used in Thai stir-fries and in Hindu religious practice. Lemon basil, purple basil and small-leaved Greek basil are other common types. They all need broadly the same care.

## Pots and soil: the foundation

### Choosing a pot

The single most important feature of a herb pot is a **drainage hole**. Without one, water collects at the bottom, the roots sit in waterlogged soil, they run short of oxygen and start to rot. Root rot is one of the most common ways potted herbs die, and it often looks like underwatering at first, because a plant with damaged roots wilts even in wet soil. If you love a decorative container with no holes, use it as an outer sleeve and put a plain plastic pot with holes inside it, emptying any water that collects.

Size matters too. Small pots dry out quickly and leave little room for roots. For a single basil plant, a pot of around 15 to 20 centimetres across and a similar depth is a reasonable minimum; bigger is easier to manage because it holds more water. A long trough of 20 centimetres or more in depth can hold several plants. Parsley, which grows a long taproot, and coriander, which dislikes being disturbed, appreciate deeper pots.

The material makes a difference:

- **Terracotta** (unglazed clay) is porous, so the soil breathes and dries out faster. That is good for Mediterranean herbs that hate wet roots, like rosemary and thyme, but means more watering for thirsty plants like basil, especially in hot, sunny spots.
- **Plastic** is light, cheap and holds moisture longer. It is often the practical choice for basil and mint.
- **Glazed ceramic** holds moisture like plastic and is heavy, which helps in windy spots.
- **Fabric grow bags** drain well and keep roots cool, but dry out quickly.

Dark-coloured pots in full tropical sun can get hot enough to stress roots. A lighter colour, or grouping pots so they shade each other, helps.

### Choosing soil

Do not fill a pot with ordinary garden soil. In the ground, soil has worms, roots and a structure built up over years that keeps it open and drained. In the confined space of a pot, garden soil tends to compact into a dense, airless lump that drains badly. Instead, use a **potting mix** made for containers. These are usually based on materials like peat, coconut coir, composted bark and perlite, and they stay light and well drained.

You can tailor the mix to the herb:

- Basil, parsley, coriander and mint like a mix that holds some moisture but drains freely, with a reasonable amount of organic matter. Mixing in some compost works well.
- Rosemary, thyme, oregano and sage, the Mediterranean group, prefer a leaner, grittier mix. Add extra perlite, coarse sand or fine gravel, perhaps a third by volume.

The old advice to put a layer of gravel or broken pottery at the bottom of a pot "for drainage" turns out to be counterproductive. Water does not move easily from fine soil into a coarse layer below, so the gravel actually raises the zone of saturated soil higher in the pot. A good mix and a drainage hole are enough. If you want to stop soil washing out, a piece of mesh or a coffee filter over the hole works.

## Starting basil: seeds, cuttings or plants

### From seed

Basil is easy to grow from seed and much cheaper than buying plants. The seeds are small and black and become coated in a slightly gelatinous layer when wet, which is normal.

1. Fill a small pot or seed tray with moist seed-starting or potting mix.
2. Scatter the seeds on the surface and cover them with only a thin layer of mix, around half a centimetre at most.
3. Keep the mix moist but not soggy. A spray bottle helps avoid washing the seeds away.
4. Keep them warm. Basil germinates best at around 20 to 25°C, and in those conditions seedlings typically appear in about a week, sometimes sooner. In cool conditions, germination is slow and patchy.
5. Once seedlings appear, give them plenty of light immediately. Seedlings in poor light stretch into thin, pale, floppy stems.
6. When they have one or two pairs of true leaves (the leaves that look like basil, as opposed to the first rounded seed leaves), thin them so the strongest plants have room, or move them to individual pots.

In tropical climates you can sow directly into the final container. Sowing a few seeds every few weeks gives you a steady supply as older plants slow down.

### From cuttings

Basil roots very easily. Cut a healthy stem about 10 centimetres long, just below a leaf node (the point where leaves join the stem). Remove the lower leaves, put the stem in a glass of water on a bright windowsill, out of harsh direct sun, and change the water every couple of days. Roots usually appear within one to two weeks. Once they are a few centimetres long, pot the cutting up. This is a good way to multiply a variety you like, including stems from a bunch bought at the market, provided they are fresh.

### Rescuing supermarket basil

The potted basil sold in supermarkets is often not one plant but a dense clump of a dozen or more seedlings sown together to look lush on the shelf. Crowded together in a small pot of exhausted soil, they compete for light, water and nutrients, and the whole clump soon collapses.

The fix is simple. Take the clump out of its pot, gently tease it into three or four smaller clumps (or even individual seedlings, if you are careful), and plant each one in its own larger pot of fresh potting mix. Water well and keep them out of strong direct sun for a few days while they recover. Many people who think they cannot keep basil alive have simply been trying to grow fifteen plants in a pot meant for one.

## Light: the thing that matters most

If there is one key to healthy herbs, it is **light**. Basil and most other culinary herbs are sun lovers. A common guideline for basil is at least six to eight hours of direct sunlight a day. With less, it grows weakly, the stems stretch, the leaves become thin and the flavour weakens.

Indoors, light is usually the limiting factor. Even a bright room is far darker than outdoors, and a few metres away from a window, light levels drop dramatically. If you are growing indoors, put herbs right next to the brightest window you have. In the northern hemisphere, that is usually a south-facing one; in the southern hemisphere, north-facing. If you do not have enough natural light, a simple LED grow light placed close above the plants and left on for 12 to 16 hours a day can make the difference.

Hot climates need a slightly different approach. In strong tropical sun, especially on a west-facing balcony that bakes in the afternoon, basil and other leafy herbs may wilt and scorch, and the soil can dry out by midday. Here, morning sun with some afternoon shade often works better. Mint, parsley, coriander, perilla and Vietnamese coriander all appreciate some protection from the harshest afternoon sun in the tropics.

Signs your herbs need more light:

- Long gaps between pairs of leaves (leggy growth).
- Stems leaning strongly toward the window.
- Pale or smaller new leaves.
- Weak flavour.

Turning pots a quarter turn every few days helps indoor plants grow evenly.

## Watering: how much, how often

Watering kills more potted herbs than anything else, both too much and too little. There is no fixed schedule that works, because the right amount depends on the plant, the pot size and material, the soil, the temperature, the sun and the wind. A small terracotta pot on a hot balcony may need watering every day, while the same plant indoors in a large plastic pot may need it once or twice a week.

The best approach is to check the soil:

1. Push a finger about two to three centimetres into the soil.
2. If it feels dry at that depth, water. If it still feels moist, wait.
3. When you water, water thoroughly until some drains out of the bottom of the pot. This makes sure the whole root zone gets wet and helps flush out salts that build up from fertiliser and tap water.
4. Empty saucers so the pot does not sit in water.

Another trick is to lift the pot. A freshly watered pot is noticeably heavier than a dry one, and after a while you will learn the difference by feel.

Different herbs have different tastes:

- **Basil** likes evenly moist soil, never soggy and never bone dry. If it dries out completely it wilts dramatically, though it usually perks up within hours of watering. Repeated drying out stresses it and can push it to flower early.
- **Mint** and **Vietnamese coriander** like consistently moist soil and tolerate wetter conditions than most.
- **Rosemary, thyme, oregano and sage** prefer the soil to dry out somewhat between waterings. Overwatering is the classic way to kill rosemary.

Water in the morning where possible, aiming at the soil rather than the leaves. Leaves that stay wet overnight, especially in humid weather, are more prone to fungal disease.

## Feeding

Potting mix contains only limited nutrients, and they wash out with watering. Herbs grown for their leaves benefit from a modest supply of nitrogen, the nutrient most associated with leafy growth. A balanced liquid fertiliser at half the label strength every two weeks or so during active growth, or a slow-release fertiliser mixed into the soil at planting, is usually plenty. Organic options include diluted fish emulsion, seaweed extract or worm castings.

Do not overdo it. Herbs that are heavily fed can grow lush but bland, because some of the aromatic oils that give herbs their flavour tend to be more concentrated in plants grown a little lean. This is especially true of the Mediterranean herbs, which often need little or no feeding at all.

## Harvesting: the secret to a bushy plant

The way you harvest basil decides whether you end up with a tall, spindly stick with a few leaves on top or a dense, bushy plant that keeps producing for months.

### Pinch from the top

Look closely at a basil stem. At each leaf node, in the angle where each leaf joins the stem, there is a tiny pair of side buds. If you cut the stem just above a node, those two buds will grow into two new stems. Each of those, cut in turn, becomes two more. That is how a basil plant becomes bushy.

So the rule is: **harvest from the top, cutting just above a pair of leaves**. Do not strip off the big lower leaves one by one, which leaves a bare stem with a tuft at the top, and do not cut the stem down to a bare stump with no leaves left, since it may not regrow.

Start pinching early. When a young plant has about three pairs of true leaves and is perhaps 15 centimetres tall, pinch off the top, just above the second or third pair. It feels harsh to cut such a small plant, but it sets up the branching structure. After that, harvest regularly, always cutting just above a node and leaving several pairs of leaves on each stem. A good rule of thumb is never to take more than about a third of the plant at once.

### Stop the flowers

Sooner or later, basil will try to flower. You will see the tip of a stem change: instead of producing a new pair of leaves, it produces a tight spike of small bracts and buds. Heat, long days, root stress and drying out all encourage flowering.

Once basil flowers and sets seed, it tends to put less energy into new leaves, growth slows and the plant eventually declines. Many cooks also find the leaves less tender and the flavour changing. To keep a plant leafy for longer, **pinch off flower spikes as soon as you see them**, cutting back to just above a pair of good leaves. Regular harvesting from the top usually removes flower buds before they form.

That said, basil flowers are edible and attract bees and other pollinators, and Thai basil flowers are pretty. If you have several plants, letting one flower is a nice compromise. You can also save seed from it, though seed from different basil varieties grown close together may not come true to type because they cross-pollinate.

### Using and storing the harvest

Basil is best used fresh. Unlike most herbs, it dislikes the cold: stored in the fridge, the leaves quickly turn black. To keep cut stems for a day or two, stand them in a glass of water at room temperature, like a bunch of flowers, out of direct sun. For longer storage, basil does not dry especially well compared with herbs like oregano, because much of its aroma is lost, but it freezes well as pesto, or chopped and covered with olive oil in ice cube trays.

## Common problems and fixes

### Yellowing leaves

Yellow leaves have several possible causes. Overwatering and poor drainage are the most common: check whether the soil stays soggy and whether the pot drains. Lower leaves yellowing on an otherwise healthy, growing plant can point to a lack of nitrogen, fixed by feeding. Cold stress and simple old age of the lowest leaves are other causes.

### Wilting

If the soil is dry, the plant is thirsty; water it. If the soil is wet and the plant still wilts, suspect root rot. Tip the plant out and look at the roots: healthy roots are white or pale and firm, rotten ones are brown, mushy and smelly. Trim off rotten roots, repot in fresh mix in a pot that drains, and water more carefully. Severely affected plants are often better replaced, perhaps by rooting healthy cuttings from them first.

### Leggy, floppy plants

The usual cause is too little light, sometimes combined with too much feeding. Move the plant somewhere brighter and cut it back to encourage bushier growth.

### Pests

Aphids (small, soft-bodied insects clustered on new growth), whiteflies, spider mites (which cause fine speckling and sometimes webbing, especially indoors in dry air), and caterpillars and slugs (which chew holes) all attack herbs. For edible plants, start with gentle methods:

- Inspect leaves, especially the undersides, regularly. Catching pests early makes them easier to deal with.
- Knock aphids off with a strong spray of water, or wipe them off by hand.
- Pick off caterpillars and slugs.
- If needed, use insecticidal soap or a horticultural oil that is labelled as suitable for edible plants, following the label, and wash leaves before eating.

Outdoors, ladybirds, lacewings, hoverflies and small wasps eat many pests, so avoiding broad-spectrum insecticides helps keep their numbers up.

### Basil downy mildew

A disease worth knowing by name is **basil downy mildew**, caused by the fungus-like organism *Peronospora belbahrii*. It has spread widely around the world since the early 2000s. The first sign is usually yellowing of leaves, often bounded by the veins, which can be mistaken for nutrient deficiency. The giveaway is on the underside of the leaves: a fuzzy, dark grey to purplish coating, especially visible after humid nights. Infected leaves eventually turn brown and drop.

The disease thrives in warm, humid conditions with wet leaves. To reduce the risk, give plants space for air to circulate, water the soil rather than the leaves, water in the morning, and choose resistant varieties if they are available where you live. If a plant becomes infected, remove and bin it rather than composting it, as the spores spread easily. Sweet basil varieties are generally more susceptible than some other types.

## Beyond basil: other herbs for pots

Once you have basil going, adding a few other herbs turns a pot or two into a proper kitchen garden.

### Mint

Mint is almost impossible to kill and very hard to contain. It spreads through underground runners and will smother neighbours if planted with them, so **always give mint its own pot**. It likes moist soil and tolerates partial shade. Cut it back hard when it gets straggly, and it will regrow fresh and tender. Many different mints exist; spearmint is the most common culinary type. In Vietnamese cooking, a spearmint type called *húng lủi* is a staple in fresh herb plates.

### Parsley

Parsley comes in curly and flat-leaf forms; flat-leaf is often preferred for flavour. Seeds are slow to germinate, often taking two to four weeks, so be patient; soaking them in warm water overnight before sowing may help. Parsley is a biennial: it grows leaves in its first year and flowers in its second, after which it declines. Harvest the outer stems from the base and let the centre keep growing.

### Coriander (cilantro)

Coriander is beloved and frustrating in equal measure. It grows fast in cool weather but **bolts**, meaning it rushes to flower and seed, as soon as temperatures rise and days lengthen. Once it bolts, the leaves become finer and less pleasant. In hot climates it is best grown in the cooler season. Tips:

- Sow seeds directly in a deep pot, since coriander dislikes being transplanted.
- Sow small batches every two to three weeks for a continuous supply.
- Give it some afternoon shade in warm weather.
- If it does bolt, let it flower: the flowers attract beneficial insects, and the seeds that follow are the spice coriander.

### Rosemary, thyme, oregano and sage

These Mediterranean herbs come from dry, sunny, rocky hillsides. They want full sun, gritty, fast-draining soil, terracotta pots, and less water than leafy herbs. Overwatering and poor drainage are their main enemies. They are perennials, woody shrubs in the case of rosemary and sage, and can last for years in a large pot. In very humid tropical climates they can struggle; good drainage, good air movement and protection from prolonged rain help.

### Chives and spring onions

Chives produce grassy, mildly oniony leaves and pretty purple flowers. Cut leaves near the base and they regrow. A related trick: the white root ends of spring onions (*hành lá*) from the market will regrow in a pot of soil, or even a glass of water for a while, giving several more harvests of green tops.

## Herbs for Vietnamese and Southeast Asian cooking

A bowl of phở, a plate of bánh xèo or a serving of bún chả comes with a basket of fresh herbs, and many of them are easy to grow in pots in warm climates, or in summer in cooler ones.

- **Vietnamese coriander** (*rau răm*, *Persicaria odorata*): a spicy, peppery herb with narrow, pointed leaves, often with a dark mark in the centre. It is not related to true coriander. It loves warmth and moist, even wet, soil and partial shade, and it grows readily from cuttings rooted in water. It does not tolerate frost. It is traditionally eaten with balut (*trứng vịt lộn*) and in chicken salad.
- **Culantro** (*ngò gai*, *Eryngium foetidum*): long, saw-edged leaves with a strong coriander-like flavour that holds up better in cooking than coriander does. It prefers partial shade and moist soil, and in strong sun it tends to flower quickly and the leaves become tough. Remove flower stalks to keep it leafy.
- **Perilla** (*tía tô*, *Perilla frutescens*): leaves green on top and purple underneath in the common Vietnamese form, with a distinctive, slightly minty, citrusy aroma. It grows quickly in warm weather and often self-seeds.
- **Vietnamese balm** (*kinh giới*, *Elsholtzia ciliata*): lemony and minty, another mint-family plant, and grown much like mint.
- **Thai basil** (*húng quế*): cared for exactly like sweet basil, and generally more tolerant of heat.
- **Fish mint** (*diếp cá*, *Houttuynia cordata*): a heart-shaped leaf with a sharp, fishy, sour taste that people tend either to love or to hate. It spreads vigorously by runners like mint, so keep it in its own pot, and it enjoys moist soil and some shade.

Many of these root easily from stems bought fresh at the market. Strip the lower leaves, stand the stems in water, and plant them when roots appear. Within a few weeks, you can have a living herb basket for the price of a bunch.

## Putting together a herb container

If you want several herbs in one large container, group plants with similar needs:

- **Leafy, thirsty herbs together**: basil, parsley, coriander, chives, perilla. Moist, rich mix; sun with some afternoon shade in hot climates.
- **Mediterranean herbs together**: rosemary, thyme, oregano, sage. Gritty, fast-draining mix; full sun; let the soil dry between waterings.
- **Spreaders alone**: mint, fish mint and, to a degree, Vietnamese coriander each in their own pots.

Put taller plants at the back or centre so they do not shade the shorter ones, and leave enough space between plants for air to move.

## A simple month-by-month mindset

Rather than a rigid calendar, which depends on your climate, think in terms of the plant's cycle:

1. **Start**: sow seeds or plant young herbs when conditions suit them: warm weather for basil and Southeast Asian herbs, cool weather for coriander and parsley in hot climates.
2. **Establish**: keep soil evenly moist, give maximum light, and pinch the tips of young basil to start branching.
3. **Harvest and maintain**: cut regularly from the top, remove flower buds, feed lightly every couple of weeks, and check for pests.
4. **Renew**: when a basil plant gets woody, sparse and keeps trying to flower, take cuttings or sow new seed and let the old plant go. Annual herbs are not meant to last forever.

## Quick answers to common questions

**Can I grow basil on a windowsill all year?** In a warm home with a bright window, yes, though growth slows in the darker months of temperate winters. A grow light helps a great deal. In the tropics, basil grows outdoors for most of the year.

**How long does a basil plant last?** With regular pinching, a healthy plant can produce for several months. Eventually it becomes woody and keeps trying to flower. At that point, start fresh from seed or cuttings.

**Should I mist my herbs?** Misting raises humidity only for a few minutes and keeps leaves wet, which can encourage disease. For most culinary herbs it is unnecessary. Watering the soil properly matters far more.

**Why does my coriander keep flowering?** It is almost always heat and long days. Sow in the cooler part of the year, give afternoon shade, and sow small batches often.

**Is it safe to eat herbs from a balcony beside a busy road?** Dust and pollution settle on leaves, so wash herbs well before eating. Growing them a little back from the street edge, behind a railing planter or a wall, can help.

## Final thoughts

Growing herbs in pots teaches you to watch closely: how a leaf looks when it is thirsty, how a stem stretches when it wants more light, how a plant changes as it gets ready to flower. The rules are simple. Use a pot that drains and a proper potting mix. Give herbs as much light as you can. Water when the soil is dry a little way down, thoroughly, and not on a fixed schedule. Harvest from the top, cutting just above a pair of leaves, and pinch out flowers. Give spreaders their own pots.

Follow those, and a single pot of basil can give you fresh leaves for months, and the occasional summer evening when you step out to the balcony, snip a few sprigs, and the whole kitchen smells of it.
